sweep_summary: Language not in catalog. The one works with stress in the title (Hargus 2003, ANLA CA982H2003) is a pre-publication typescript of Hargus 2005 (Athabaskan Prosody 393-423) and is about Witsuwit'en (and Ft. Ware Sekani) word stress; the ANLA hosts an open PDF (found via the archive's JSON API and file list; TLS cert on uafanlc.alaska.edu fails verification, downloaded by automated download -k) and it was downloaded, read, and logged at It gives a first-hand, acoustically verified, ranked parameter system: stem > peripheral/long vowel > closed syllable > word-initial, with Witsuwit'en explicitly non-tonal. This agrees with Hargus 2001 (already held by the project, read: left-aligned trochaic quantity-sensitive feet, weight VV > V(C) > əC > ə) and with the second-hand summaries in Gessner 2003 and Story 1989 noted in the earlier reading. Not obtained: the Benjamins 2005 version (paywalled; same content) and Hargus 2007 Witsuwit'en Grammar ch. 20 (print; medium priority).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable (p. 42: parameters are stem vs affix, peripheral vs central vowel, long vs short, left word edge, closed vs open syllable). Default is left-edge: trochaic quantity-sensitive feet built from the left, so main stress is word-initial when non-final syllables have full (peripheral) vowels; a syllable with central ə is skipped in favour of a following peripheral-vowel or closed syllable (prefix ə + stem disyllables stress the stem; ə.əC.. stresses the second syllable, otherwise the first); long peripheral vowels attract main stress even word-medially, leftmost long vowel winning. Weight scale VV > V(C) > əC > ə. Stems outrank affixes (2016 slides: 'in case of conflict, stress-root most important').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Word-final (stem) syllable carries secondary stress in longer all-peripheral words (p. 43); footing examples show alternating secondary stresses on non-head feet, e.g. (nə́c'ə)(bə̀yə)nə(tə̀n); medial-syllable stress status called debatable.
new_statements.exceptions: Central vowel ə in an initial syllable is never stressed in prefix+stem disyllables; closed əC counts as heavy only relative to open ə (an open peripheral-vowel syllable still beats a closed ə syllable, ex. 40); long peripheral vowels override the left-edge default (ex. 41-42); morphological stem-vs-affix parameter listed but deferred to Hargus in prep. (= 2007 grammar).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on inflected words (mostly verbs) in citation form; author notes experimental verification of some parameters in Hargus (in preparation = 2005/2007). Full treatment is ch. 20 'Stress' of Hargus 2007, which this article anticipates.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand statements found describe the Witsuwit'en (western, Bulkley Valley / Moricetown-Witset) dialect of Babine-Witsuwit'en (babi1235; Glottolog dialect witsuwiten / 'Witsuwit'en'). The eastern Babine (Lake Babine, Nedut'en) dialect is described for phonology by Story 1984 (not opened); Story 1989 remarks second-hand that in Babine a short/long vowel distinction is needed to predict stress.

new_statements.quote: The primary, or least violable, stress parameter is morphological category: as noted above, stress falls on stem syllables even when such syllables contain the central vowel [ə] [...]. Vowel quantity is the next most important parameter, accounting for primary stress on the non-final, prefix syllable in ['yexʷi,dəc] "you (pl.) are talking". The closed syllable parameter determines stress placement in sequences of prefixes containing [ə] [...]. In such cases, stress is attracted to closed syllables. Finally, in prefix sequences containing open syllable /ə/, stress falls on the leftmost, or word initial, syllable.

new_statements.reading: Witsuwit'en is non-tonal and word stress is predictable, not lexical. Ranking: (1) the stem syllable is always stressed (in verbs the stem is word-final); (2) among prefix syllables, a peripheral (non-schwa) or long vowel attracts stress, the leftmost long vowel winning; (3) among schwa prefixes, a closed syllable attracts stress (LH[stem] words stress the second syllable); (4) otherwise stress falls on the word-initial syllable. In polysyllables with all peripheral vowels primary stress is transcribed on the initial syllable with secondary stress on the final stem; acoustically the stem stress is the robust one, word-initial stress is weak and inconsistent across speakers (p. 16). Equivalent to Hargus 2001's left-aligned trochaic quantity-sensitive feet with weight scale VV > V(C) > əC > ə. For a catalog's classification: morphologically conditioned (stem-dominant) weight-sensitive stress with a leftmost default and no lexical contrast.

The only sentence of the Introduction seen (Google Books snippet, p. 37) characterises Witsuwit'en as a non-tonal language with word stress whose phonetic correlates Hargus studies in the same volume; p. 35 (snippet) makes the family-wide point that the stem syllable is more prominent than affixes.
new_statements.identity_note: All catalog statements (Hargus 2001, 2003/2005) describe Witsuwit'en, the western dialect of Babine-Witsuwit'en, from Hargus's own fieldwork; the Introduction snippet likewise names Witsuwit'en. Story 1984 (Babine, eastern dialect) is not among the listed works and was not opened; Hargus 2005 p. 404 (snippet) notes that Story 1984 does not report word-initial stress for Babine-Witsuwit'en, so the western-dialect transcription of word-initial primary stress is Hargus's and may not carry over to Babine.

Stress is predictable from five parameters, table (6) p. 7: stems (vs affixes); peripheral /i e a o u/ (vs central schwa); long (vs short) peripheral vowels; left edge of word (vs medial); closed (vs open) syllables. Ranked in (17) p. 12: stem > vowel quantity (peripheral/long) > closed syllable > word-initial (least important).
